sources.title: Duffy, Lai, and Lim, Coordination via Correlation: An Experimental Study (2017)
sources.supports: Public correlated selection, distinction from independent mixing, learning direct versus indirect signals, and alternation with fixed partners.
sources.read_method: Author-hosted published PDF introduction, formal framework, procedures, and reported findings read. Earlier author version also inspected. Bibliographic record identifies Economic Theory 64 (2017), 265–304; online publication/copyright 2016.
sources.boundary: 214 HKUST undergraduates in 60-round sessions; random matching within groups or fixed pairs. The experiment uses specified monetary payoffs; the article instead states qualitative venue preferences. No experimental rates transferred to the article. Shared signals require common interpretation; the research does not establish automatic compliance or acceptance of any public lottery.

patterns.short_description: Recognize when everyone prefers agreement to a split but favors a different agreement, then distinguish coordinating actions from deciding whose preference prevails.
use_when: How can both want to meet while favoring different plans?
Nia prefers a film and Theo a concert. Both prefer either shared activity to separate evenings.
goals: Recognize the familiar predicament before specialist terminology.
Explain the defining mechanism and distinguish neighboring concepts.

One-shot choices without seeing the other’s current choice; preferences and feasible options known. No future rewards or binding commitment in the initial game. One person still accepts a less preferred evening.
Separate hypothetical behavior, model results, documented cases, and practical editorial proposals.
mechanisms: One accepted shared draw and acknowledged activity select an existing matching equilibrium.
Both activities must be feasible and acceptable. One person still receives the less preferred outcome.

visual.question: How can both want to meet while favoring different plans?
visual.alternative_text: Hypothetical qualitative illustration. Nia prefers a film, Theo a concert, and both prefer either shared activity to separate evenings. Together at the film and together at the concert are the two double-outlined equilibria. A shared acknowledged draw can select one. Change: Agree one shared selection and confirm the same activity before departing. Limitation: Both activities must be feasible and acceptable. One person still receives the less preferred outcome.
visual.caption: Hypothetical illustration. Compare Nia’s and Theo’s activity choices. Matching choices keep them together but favor different people. A shared draw selects an existing equilibrium; equal chances do not give both their preferred evening or settle fairness.
